name: Chiropractic adjustments

lead: A chiropractic adjustment is a quick manual thrust applied to spinal joints. People seek it for back and neck discomfort and some hope it straightens the spine for better posture and frame.

The chain is manipulated spinal joints, reduced stiffness or discomfort, then easier upright posture. Reviews summarized on Wikipedia report modest or low-certainty benefits for some back and neck pain and no good evidence for non-musculoskeletal conditions. No study was found testing lasting posture or appearance change.

paras: A licensed chiropractor applies a high-velocity, low-amplitude thrust to a joint, often over a series of visits and sometimes alongside exercises or stretches. Chiropractic theory attributes effects to correcting subluxations, a concept described as unsubstantiated.

Soreness and headache are common and temporary. Rare serious events, including stroke after neck manipulation, are reported, and causality is debated. The profession is licensed in most places; people with neck pain, bone conditions or on blood thinners may want to discuss it with a doctor first.

angle.text: People seek chiropractic adjustments hoping to ease spinal stiffness and straighten posture and frame. The path runs from manipulated joints to less stiffness to easier upright posture. Trials have looked at back and neck pain with low-certainty benefit; lasting posture change has not been shown.

lead: A chiropractic adjustment is a manual intervention, most often a high-velocity, low-amplitude thrust, applied to the joints of the spine; chiropractors use "adjustment" for what clinical literature calls spinal manipulation [1][2]. It is the core technique of chiropractic, a profession founded in the 1890s by the Canadian-born magnetic healer D. D. Palmer [1][3].

People seek adjustments mostly for back and neck pain, but in lifting, bodybuilding and posture circles they are also discussed as a way to restore alignment, relieve tightness that limits training and stand or sit taller. The appearance chain proposed by practitioners and clients is: spinal joints moved, so stiffness and pain ease, so posture, range of motion and training capacity improve, so the frame looks more upright and the physique develops more fully. Chiropractors also give ergonomic advice and exercise guidance alongside adjustments [1].

Research on adjustments centres on pain and disability. A 2017 American College of Physicians guideline lists spinal manipulation among non-drug options for low back pain, citing low-quality evidence [4]; a 2026 randomized trial compared manipulation and self-management for acute back pain [5]. Reviews summarized on Wikipedia report modest or low-certainty benefits for some back and neck pain and no good evidence for non-musculoskeletal conditions, while safety discussions centre on rare serious events after neck manipulation [1][2].

paras: Spinal manipulation is applied to the synovial joints of the spine, most often for low back pain, and is performed mainly by chiropractors, osteopaths and physical therapists; chiropractors call it an adjustment [2]. It is commonly described as a high-velocity, low-amplitude thrust, equivalent to Grade V mobilization in Maitland's system, and is defined by joint gapping that can produce cavitation in synovial fluid, the source of the audible "crack" [2].

Adjustments are delivered by hand or with instruments such as the Activator. Common schools include Diversified (the most widely used), Activator, Gonstead, Thompson, Cox flexion-distraction and Sacro-Occipital Technique [1]. A US survey cited on Wikipedia found over 10 percent of patients receiving each of several named techniques [1]. Chiropractors also offer exercise advice, ergonomic guidance and soft-tissue work [1].

Manipulation has roots in folk bone-setting and is attributed in lore to Hippocrates and ancient Egypt; its modern form emerged in late 19th-century North America alongside osteopathy [2]. Daniel David Palmer (1845 to 1913), born in Ontario and a magnetic healer in Iowa, claimed in 1895 that he restored the hearing of a Davenport janitor, Harvey Lillard, by manipulating his back; Lillard's daughter later gave a different account [3]. Palmer opened the Palmer School and Cure in Davenport in 1897 [3]. In 1906 he was prosecuted for practising medicine without a licence and served 17 days in jail rather than pay the fine; he then sold the school to his son B. J. Palmer [3].

Palmer's subluxation theory held that spinal misalignments interfere with nerve function and general health. Wikipedia reports that Palmer first proposed pinched nerves and later altered nerve vibration, that the World Health Organization in 2005 described the subluxation as a functional rather than structural lesion, and that the UK General Chiropractic Council states the concept is not supported by clinical research evidence [1]. Chiropractors divide into "straights", who keep the original vitalistic philosophy, and "mixers", who combine it with science; most practitioners are mixers [1]. A 2008 critical evaluation in the Journal of Pain and Symptom Management described this internal conflict and argued that subluxation and spinal manipulation as core concepts are not based on sound science [6].

The American Medical Association called chiropractic an "unscientific cult" in 1966 and boycotted it until losing the antitrust case Wilk v. AMA in 1987; from the late 20th century chiropractic gained more acceptance from physicians and US health plans [1].

Researchers have proposed that manipulation produces temporary pain relief, increased range of motion, effects on the sympathetic nervous system and altered sensorimotor processing [2]. A 2021 narrative review in the European Journal of Pain reported that spinal cord mechanisms of pain inhibition contribute at least partly to the pain-relieving effect, with weaker evidence for peripheral and supraspinal mechanisms, and called for validated placebo interventions [7]. Wikipedia notes a 1998 study finding that manipulation did not alter sacroiliac joint position, which bears on the "putting a bone back" idea [2].

sections.h: Use in lifting and posture communities
paras: Strength-training forums mention chiropractors mainly as a response to acute back, rib or shoulder problems that stop training. Users describe getting "aligned" before a massage, having ribs "put back" after a lifting injury, or having a shoulder issue relieved in a single visit [8][9][10]. Others report ambivalence: one user wrote that they could not understand why people enjoy the experience, and another recalled gym talk that chiropractic patients are always told they need further treatment [11][12].

In appearance terms, the claims centre on posture: correcting forward head carriage, rounded shoulders or uneven hips so the body looks more upright. Chiropractors in these threads often pair the adjustment with strengthening advice, such as working the glute medius [8]. No controlled study has tested adjustments for aesthetic posture or facial appearance outcomes.

A 2018 US National Center for Health Statistics data brief tracked adults' use of yoga, meditation and chiropractors [13]. A 1997 Canadian survey examined use of alternative health practitioners, including chiropractors [14], and population studies from the 1990s examined care-seeking for severe and chronic low back pain, a leading reason people see chiropractors [15]. A 2026 JAMA review states that low back pain affects about 619 million people worldwide and is the leading cause of years lived with disability [16].

For low back pain, a 2012 Cochrane review cited on Wikipedia found manipulation no more effective than placebo for acute pain, while a 2019 meta-analysis found results comparable to recommended treatments for chronic pain [2]. The 2017 American College of Physicians guideline recommended spinal manipulation among non-drug options for acute, subacute and chronic low back pain, rating the evidence low quality [4]. A 2011 review of 45 systematic reviews concluded that spinal manipulation had not been convincingly shown effective for any condition [1], and Wikipedia reports a Cochrane review finding small to moderate short-term benefit for chronic low back pain versus sham or no treatment, with little difference from other conservative therapies [1].

The PACBACK trial (JAMA, 2026) randomized 1,000 adults with acute or subacute low back pain at risk of chronic disability to spinal manipulation, clinician-supported self-management, both, or guideline-based medical care. Self-management alone and combined with manipulation reduced disability significantly more than medical care; manipulation alone did not differ significantly from medical care, and pain differences were small [5]. A 2025 systematic review examined whether adding manual therapy, including spinal manipulation, to exercise improves outcomes in chronic low back pain over exercise alone [17].

For neck pain, a 2015 Cochrane review found no high-quality evidence, with low-to-moderate quality evidence that several sessions may relieve pain compared with some medications [2]. Randomized trials have examined manipulation for lumbar disc herniation with radiculopathy [18], subacute and chronic lumbar radiculopathy [19], chronic cervical radiculopathy combined with exercise [20] and tension-type headache with neck pain [21]. A 2024 chapter reviewed physical treatments for migraine [22]. A 2019 review found no evidence of benefit for non-musculoskeletal conditions such as asthma or migraine [2].

A 1987 pilot study of nine patients with sacroiliac dysfunction used a force platform to measure gait symmetry before and after chiropractic manipulation [23]. No controlled study was found testing adjustments for aesthetic posture or facial appearance outcomes.

Mild temporary effects such as soreness, headache and fatigue are common, estimated at 33 to 61 percent of patients; the WHO has described chiropractic as generally safe when practised skilfully [1]. Rare serious events, including stroke from vertebral artery dissection, have been associated mainly with neck manipulation, and whether the link is causal is disputed [1][2]. Reported estimates range from 5 strokes per 100,000 manipulations to 2.68 deaths per 10 million, and under-reporting makes incidence hard to estimate [1][2].

A 2001 Ontario case-control study of 582 vertebrobasilar accident cases found that in people under 45 the cases were about five times as likely as controls to have visited a chiropractor within the previous week, with no significant association at 45 and over; the authors noted possible bias and the rarity of the events [24]. A 2008 Ontario study of 818 cases found under-45 cases about three times as likely to have seen either a chiropractor or a primary care physician before the stroke; the authors concluded the pattern probably reflects people with early dissection seeking care for headache and neck pain, and reported no excess risk compared with primary care [25].

Wikipedia also notes that some critics advise caution about full-spine X-rays, and that anti-vaccine views are prevalent among some chiropractors, which has drawn criticism from public-health bodies [1].

In the United States chiropractors hold a Doctor of Chiropractic degree and are licensed by state, with accredited programmes requiring undergraduate study; Canada, Australasia and Europe have their own accredited programmes, and in the UK the General Chiropractic Council regulates the profession [1]. Chiropractors are not M.D.s or D.O.s [1].

lore.intro: On lifting forums such as T Nation, chiropractors come up mostly as a fix for acute injuries and nagging aches, with opinions ranging from enthusiasm to wariness about ongoing treatment plans [8][11][12].
